name: Skin-tone matching foundation / BB cream for men

card.summary: Light base makeup used to even out skin tone; mainstream in cosmetics, with little research on male appearance outcomes.
card.aka: BB cream, blemish balm, tinted moisturizer, CC cream
card.note: Shade matching varies between brands, and no clinical studies of male use were found.

lead: Skin-tone matching foundation and BB cream are tinted base products applied to the face to even out complexion and cover blemishes. Men use them to reduce the look of redness, acne marks, scars and dark under-eyes in a single quick step, usually with a sheer, natural finish. Foundation is a long-established cosmetic category, while BB cream ("blemish balm" or "beauty balm") is a lighter hybrid intended to combine coverage, moisturizer and sun protection.[1][2]

BB cream was reportedly first formulated in Germany in the 1960s by the dermatologist Christine Schrammek for skin after facial peels and surgery, and was developed for daily use by South Korean companies in the 1980s. Western brands launched versions from about 2012, and some critics said these were essentially tinted moisturizers.[1] Korean brands began selling men's versions around 2010, and men's cosmetics were largely absent from mainstream Western markets until the late 1990s.[3][10]

The appearance case rests on how people read faces. A 2012 study of male cheek skin found that photographs with more even melanin and hemoglobin distribution were rated as younger, healthier and more attractive, which is the quality a tinted base imitates.[11] On looksmax.org, BB cream and tinted moisturizer are a recurring topic: users describe them as a fast way to even tone and soften visible scars or pimples, and discuss how to choose a shade and make a tint last through the day.[4][5] No clinical studies on the effect of wearing base makeup on perceived male attractiveness were found.

chain: Tinted base matched to skin undertone
More uniform-looking complexion, which observers in studies rate as healthier and more attractive
angle.text: A shade-matched sheer base evens out tone and covers redness, blemishes and dark circles for the day it is worn. Forum users describe a "filter" effect from a small amount, with shade matching deciding how natural it looks.

paras: Foundation is a liquid, cream or powder applied to the face and neck to even out the complexion and, usually, to cover flaws or alter the natural skin tone. Formulas include oil or emollient-based, alcohol-based, powder, mineral, water-based and silicone-based types. Oil-based products are thick and opaque and can smudge or darken over time, alcohol-based ones are very light and sheer, powders can look dry or cakey on dry skin, and water-based formulas range from dewy to matte and transfer-resistant.[2]

Coverage is described in four levels: sheer products even the tone slightly, light products cover mild unevenness but not freckles, medium products cover freckles, discoloration and minor marks, and full coverage hides birthmarks and scars. Finishes run from flat matte to dewy. Applicators include fingers (suited to sheer looks), damp sponges, brushes and airbrushes.[2]

BB creams are usually designed as a light-coverage product combining skincare traits such as moisturizer and sunscreen. Many are formulated to oxidize on skin to approximate the wearer's tone, because Korean brands initially offered few shades, and some brands include brightening, soothing or anti-wrinkle claims.[1] The later CC cream puts more emphasis on color correction, and cushion compacts, which hold liquid base in a sponge, are a Korean format now sold in men's versions.[1][13]

Shade names are not standardized between brands, so a name like "Medium Beige" can vary widely. Shades are commonly classified by undertone (warm, neutral, olive or cool), and the color in the bottle can look different on skin, so testing in person is advised.[2] Some people deliberately choose a slightly different shade to counter redness, sallowness or dullness, and color correctors are used for discoloration.[2] Some brands offer limited ranges, which can make matching harder for people with darker skin.[2]

Forum users report the same issue in practice, for example a poster describing a BB cream that came out a shade above their natural tone, and threads comparing complexion shades.[6] Because many BB creams oxidize toward the wearer's tone and are sold in few shades, a sheer layer is what lets one shade work across a range of complexions.[1]

Complexion cosmetics date to antiquity. Ancient Egyptian men wore dark eye makeup, Roman men used white lead powder and chalk to lighten skin, and powdered pale makeup was widespread among men under Elizabeth I and in eighteenth-century France, when lead- and mercury-based products caused serious harm.[2][3] Max Factor's Pan-Cake, patented in 1937, is described as the first commercially sold foundation, and film in the 1930s revived popular interest in men's cosmetics.[2][3]

Men's beauty products were scarce in mainstream markets until the late 1990s and were regarded as a niche.[3] The modern male BB cream traces to Korea. Wikipedia credits the German dermatologist Christine Schrammek with the first formulation in the 1960s, for patients' skin after peels and surgery, and Korean companies with daily-use versions in the 1980s, which spread through Korean beauty trends. BB creams held about 13 percent of South Korea's cosmetics market in 2011.[1]

A November 2011 Korea JoongAng Daily article said Korea led the world in male skincare spending, with Euromonitor putting Korean men's skin care purchases at about 284.6 million euros in 2010. It reported that men bought BB cream for light coverage along with sun protection, moisturizing and whitening, that AmorePacific's Laneige Homme had introduced a men's BB cream in April 2010, and that Biotherm Homme and Lab Series were launching their own.[10] A Lab Series executive quoted there said men did not want to look made up, so the product was made very light with minimal tint.[10]

sections.h: Korea and the spread of men's base makeup
paras: Korea's role is the main driver of the category in accounts of its history. Wikipedia's entry on male grooming says competition in a tight job market has pushed Korean men toward cosmetics, that K-pop and "flower boy" idols changed perceptions of men's makeup, and that the Korean men's cosmetics market grew from 733 billion won in 2010 to 1.23 trillion won in 2018.[14] Wikipedia's article on Korean cosmetics notes that some Korean men use BB or CC cream, with men's products often built around soothing skin after daily shaving.[15]

In 2019 Inside Retail Asia, relaying Korea Bizwire, reported that a Seoul National University consumer trend survey found about three in ten Gen Z men used face makeup more than twice a week. The health and beauty chain Olive Young reported a 77 percent rise in male tinted cosmetics sales in the first half of 2019, and sales of men's cushion, BB and CC products across the market were up 43 percent from a year earlier. AmorePacific launched a men's makeup brand, BeReady, that year.[16]

Wikipedia's account of China says a trend toward softer male aesthetics and online beauty creators raised interest, with BB cream among popular products, and it cites a 2018 livestream in which the streamer Li Jiaqi sold 15,000 lipsticks in five minutes.[14][3]

In the West, Mintel reported that UK men's BB cream use roughly doubled in 2013-14 from a small base, and that men appeared to be using products marketed to women because men's BB creams were scarce on UK shelves. Mintel's guidance to brands was to favor subtle color and skincare-style positioning, since makeup still carried feminine associations for many men.[13]

An Ipsos survey published in 2022 found that 15 percent of heterosexual US men aged 18 to 65 currently used male cosmetics or makeup and a further 17 percent would consider it. Seventy-three percent of men 51 and over said they would not consider cosmetics, against 37 percent of men 18 to 34, and younger men were more open to products like BB or CC cream, foundation, concealer, bronzer and mascara. Top motivations among younger men included improving skin texture and appearance.[12]

A Morning Consult report found that one-third of young US men said they would consider wearing makeup, compared with 23 percent of all men, and that men most often wanted cover-up, concealer and tinted moisturizer. It named small direct-to-consumer men's brands, including Formen and Stryx, whose products include concealers and a tinted moisturizer, and quoted founders as saying stigma was easing among younger consumers.[18]

Wikipedia's article on male cosmetics adds that men's cosmetics packaging tends toward muted colors, that male beauty YouTubers such as Patrick Starr and James Charles have grown the audience for tutorials, and that surveys it cites found far more men use skincare than consider makeup important.[3]

Community posts describe BB cream as an easy step to hide scars, pimples and dark under-eyes. One poster wrote that scars and pimples "disappeared" with a fingertip of product and looked natural.[4] Others ask how BB cream differs from tinted sunscreen and which lasts longer, since users want a base that does not rub off easily.[5][7]

Some threads present tinted moisturizer as a habit once started, while a user with acne asked whether BB cream might irritate skin.[8][9] Views in these communities differ on whether makeup belongs in looksmaxxing, and some users frame light tint as grooming rather than makeup. Similar framing appears in brand marketing, where sheer, skincare-like products are positioned so that wearers look natural rather than made up.[10][13]
No studies found on wearing foundation or BB cream and how men are perceived.

Related research examines the skin-evenness cue that these products imitate. In a 2012 study in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology, Fink and colleagues took cheek images of 160 British Caucasian men aged 10 to 70, had 308 participants rate them for age, health and attractiveness, and measured melanin and hemoglobin evenness with an image-analysis algorithm. More even distributions were linked to looking younger, healthier and more attractive. Evenness of melanin was the stronger cue for perceived age, while evenness of hemoglobin was more closely tied to perceived health and attractiveness.[11] The study measured natural skin, not makeup, and used a single population.

A 2021 study cited by Wikipedia found organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS compounds, in more than half of 231 tested cosmetic products, with foundations among those with high levels in 63 percent of tested products. PFAS are often not listed on labels, and the article notes they can be absorbed through the skin.[2]

Forum users also raise skin irritation and breakouts as a consideration when covering acne.[9] Wikipedia notes that some emollient-based foundations can clog pores while alcohol-based ones rarely do.[2] Guides from dermatology-oriented retailers and publications commonly point to non-comedogenic labeling and lightweight formulas for oily or acne-prone skin, and to tinted products with SPF; these are general guidance rather than trial results.
Historical lead and mercury cosmetics caused serious harm, a reason foundation history is often cited alongside present-day ingredient regulation.[2][3]

Related items include concealer and color correctors for under-eyes, tinted sunscreen, tinted lip balm, eyebrow pencils and skincare routines. The Inside Retail Asia report notes that sunscreen and lip balm were top sellers for a new Korean men's brand, and that men's color lip balm and eyebrow products were popular at Olive Young.[16] Morning Consult's report also lists men's concealer and tinted moisturizer as the products men most wanted to try.[18]

lore.intro: Tinted base products are discussed in looksmaxxing spaces as an easy cosmetic way to even skin tone, with views split over whether makeup belongs in the practice.[4][5]

claims.claim: Light BB cream evens skin tone and hides scars, redness or pimples in a natural-looking way.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster said a fingertip of BB cream made scars and pimples vanish and looked like a "filter".[4] Others recommend it for dark under-eyes.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes BB creams as light-coverage products designed to conceal blemishes and match skin tone.[1] Research shows that more even skin color is rated healthier and more attractive on bare faces, but no studies were found testing how male wearers are perceived.[11]

claims.claim: A properly shade-matched product is hard to detect, while a mismatched one is obvious.
claims.believers: Users say the right undertone is the key; one poster asked for help after a product came out a shade too dark.[6]
claims.experts: Shade names vary between brands and undertones are classified as warm, neutral, olive or cool.[2]

claims.claim: Tinted sunscreen or a long-wear tint can replace BB cream for people who want it to last.
claims.believers: A poster asked for something that does not come off as easily as BB cream but gives the same effect, and others compare it with tinted sunscreen.[5][7]
claims.experts: BB creams are described as combining moisturizer and sun protection in one product.[1] No comparative studies were found.

claims.claim: Men should not look "made up", so a sheer, barely tinted product is the right approach.
claims.believers: Brand executives quoted in 2011 said men did not want to look made up, and community posters describe light tints as grooming rather than makeup.[10][8]
claims.experts: Mintel advised brands to use subtle color and skincare-style positioning because makeup still carried feminine associations for many men.[13]

claims.claim: Tinted products are mainstream in Korea and spreading to Western men.
claims.believers: Posters and brands point to Korean idols and the Korean market as the model for men's base makeup.[16]
claims.experts: Market surveys report rising use among younger men in Korea and the US, with a clear generation gap, but most figures come from commercial research firms.[12][16][18]

claims.claim: BB cream can irritate acne-prone skin.
claims.believers: A user with acne asked whether using BB cream to look clear would irritate skin.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes some emollient-based foundations can clog pores while alcohol-based ones rarely do; no trials of BB cream in male acne were found.[2]
